parsed_answer.content: Java 21 introduced Virtual Threads (Project Loom) as a paradigm shift in how we handle concurrency. Unlike Platform Threads, which are thin wrappers around OS-level threads (1:1 mapping), Virtual Threads are lightweight, user-mode threads managed by the JVM (M:N mapping). A Platform Thread is expensive, typically consuming 1MB of stack space and requiring a costly kernel context switch when blocked. In contrast, Virtual Threads are 'cheap'—they are multiplexed onto a small pool of carrier threads (the ForkJoinPool.commonPool() by default). When a Virtual Thread performs a blocking I/O operation, the JVM unmounts it from the carrier thread, allowing the carrier to execute other tasks, and remounts the Virtual Thread once the I/O completes. This solves the 'thread-per-request' scalability bottleneck, allowing applications to handle millions of concurrent tasks without exhausting system resources.

items: Virtual Threads are not intended to be pooled. Because they are lightweight, you should create a new one for every task, effectively treating threads as disposable objects rather than expensive resources.

The JVM uses a 'carrier thread' (a platform thread) to execute the code inside a virtual thread. If you execute synchronized blocks or native methods, the carrier thread is 'pinned', meaning it cannot be unmounted, which can lead to performance degradation.
Virtual Threads are daemon threads by nature. They cannot be changed to non-daemon, and their priority is always set to Thread.NORM_PRIORITY.
The underlying scheduler is a FIFO work-stealing ForkJoinPool, which ensures that carrier threads stay busy even when individual virtual threads are waiting on network or file I/O.

parsed_answer.content: Watch out for 'Thread Pinning'. If your code enters a synchronized block or calls a native method while performing blocking I/O, the JVM cannot unmount the virtual thread from the carrier thread. This effectively turns your virtual thread into a platform thread for the duration of that block, potentially leading to thread starvation in high-concurrency scenarios. Use ReentrantLock instead of synchronized blocks to avoid pinning.
